# What rimsky can do

Rimsky is a reactive node-graph orchestration platform. You write a template that declares nodes, what each node subscribes to, and what claims it takes; you deploy the template and create an instance; rimsky dispatches work as state changes cascade through the graph. Rimsky runs the graph, holds the claims, and keeps the record. Your executors do the work.

This document lists what rimsky does at this release, and which surface you drive each capability through. Each section ends with **Where rimsky differs from what you would expect** — behaviour that a reasonable reading of the surface gets wrong. Read those before you write a script against a surface.

## The surfaces

Rimsky exposes eight public surfaces. Every capability below names the ones that reach it.

| Surface | What it is | Size at this release |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | The `rimsky` binary: a thin HTTP client over the control API, plus two self-hosting one-shot modes | 93 verbs and subcommands, 77 flags |
| Control API | The JSON HTTP surface under `/v1` | 92 public routes, counting the supervisor's callback routes and the `sensor-webhook` ingress |
| MCP | A second protocol skin on the control API's port, at `/v1/mcp` | 57 tools, 5 methods, 2 resource URIs |
| gRPC protocols | The contracts your own services implement | 10 proto files, 9 services, 36 RPCs |
| Templates | The `rimsky.yml` a template author writes | 58 keys, plus 60 attribute keys across the bundled executors |
| Deployment config | The YAML an operator writes, plus `RIMSKY_*` environment variables | 57 config keys, 35 bundled-service config keys, 86 variables |
| Compose manifests | A declarative multi-resource manifest the CLI reconciles | 19 keys |
| Images and packages | What you deploy and what you build against | 15 images, 8 binaries, 9 published packages |

Two more surfaces carry their own vocabulary: 49 permission actions name what a grant covers — 46 of them grantable — and 44 event kinds plus 28 error classes name what shows up in the record.

## Running a deployment

**Rimsky runs as one process or as three.** The `rimsky` image carries all role binaries. Give the container no command and it runs the scheduler, the supervisor, and the control API in one process. Give it `rimsky-scheduler`, `rimsky-supervisor`, or `rimsky-control-api` and it runs that role alone, so you can split the three across containers and scale them separately.

**Schema migrations run exactly once, whatever the split.** The all-in-one path always migrates before the roles start. In a split deployment only the `rimsky-control-api` container migrates, so three containers do not race and do not skip it. `RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE=1` forces the step and `=0` skips it; any other value stops the container with the value named.

**The all-in-one image runs with no configuration at all.** `rimsky-all-in-one` bakes SQLite defaults, keeps its state under the `/var/lib/rimsky` volume, and serves the control API on 8080. Mount that volume and templates, instances, and event history survive a container restart.

**A load balancer or Kubernetes probe can ask whether a deployment is healthy without a credential.** `GET /v1/health` is unauthenticated and tracks persistence, so it reports unhealthy when the database is gone rather than answering from a happy path. `rimsky health` asks the same question from the CLI.

**One template file runs unedited against both deployment modes.** The same file you drive through a standing stack also runs under the CLI's self-hosted one-shot mode.

**Persistence is Postgres or SQLite.** `persistence.driver` selects it. An attribute bag and a node-run's scratch are byte columns in their own rows, whatever their size, so a deployment configures no separate store.

Driven through: the images and their commands, deployment config, `RIMSKY_*` variables, `GET /v1/health`, `rimsky health`.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **The published images are `linux/arm64` only.** All fifteen images carry exactly one platform, and none is a multi-platform index. The CLI release archives do ship `linux` and `darwin` for both `amd64` and `arm64`, so the CLI covers x86-64 and the images do not. An x86-64 host finds out at `docker run`.
- **Environment variables do not override arbitrary config keys.** A fixed, enumerated set of variables configures a deployment — `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_PORT` really does move the listener. Guessed names such as `RIMSKY_PERSISTENCE_DRIVER` or `RIMSKY_PERSISTENCE_SQLITE_PATH` change nothing and are not mentioned in the startup log. Configure a container by mounting a config file; `${VAR}` references inside that file do interpolate from the container's environment.
- **A misspelled variable is silent; a misspelled YAML key is loud.** Rimsky validates the values of variables it reads and never checks the names of variables it does not. An unknown YAML key stops the process at load with the offending key named.
- **`rimsky-migrate` is not a role name and migrations do not roll back.** `docker run … rimsky-migrate` exits non-zero, because the entrypoint reads its argument as a role. Run the migrate binary as a one-shot init container by overriding the image's entrypoint, and set `RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE=0` on the role containers so they leave the schema alone. Re-running a migrate is safe. There is no down direction anywhere: no verb, no flag, no reverse migration.
- **The SQLite driver prints a local-development-only warning at every boot.** Graph behaviour matches across the two drivers.
- **`RIMSKY_LOG_LEVEL` reaches the core roles and the host-daemon proxy only.** None of the eleven bundled services honours it. The accepted values are `debug`, `warn`, and `error`; anything else, including `DEBUG` or `trace`, falls back to the default silently.
- **Only the three core roles serve Prometheus metrics.** They serve them on their own metrics ports, not as a route on the control API's port. No bundled service serves metrics anywhere, and the metrics variables are inert on all of them.
- **`GET /health` exists on two listeners, not on every process.** The supervisor's callback listener and the `sensor-webhook` ingress answer it. The control API answers `/v1/health`, and the claude-agent HTTP bridge answers `/healthz`. The OpenLineage subscriber and the proxy's daemon-facing port serve no HTTP at all, so one probe spec does not fit every pod.
- **No two shipped default ports collide.** Core listeners take 8080 through 8099 and the bundled services take 9000 through 9199, so the whole bundle runs in one namespace at its defaults. A fitness check fails the build when a default leaves its block or two coincide.
- **`dispatch_defaults` covers three timing keys, not retry policy.** `sync_rpc_deadline`, `max_quiet_period`, and `max_runtime` have deployment-wide forms. `max_retries` and `retry_backoff` do not, and adding them stops the deployment before it starts. Retry policy is per-node.

## Access control

**A fresh deployment is open until you mint the first key.** With zero api-key rows, rimsky is in anonymous mode: every operator action answers with no credential presented, and the log carries a warning banner saying so. `rimsky auth init` mints the first admin key and shuts the door in the same act — the next unauthenticated read answers 401. Revoking the last key refuses with 409 unless you ask for it with `?force_leave_anonymous=true`.

**Rimsky administers the whole api-key lifecycle.** You create scoped keys, list them without exposing plaintext, inspect one key's grant, revoke a key, rotate one while its holder still uses the old one within a grace window, and ask the deployment which auth posture it is in.

**A grant is a list of actions, optionally scoped.** Six bundled roles — `admin`, `agent-supervisor`, `debug-operator`, `operator`, `publisher-service`, `read-only` — expand into grants at key-creation time. `--add` and `--remove` adjust an expanded role. Wildcards `*`, `<noun>:*`, and `*:<verb>` are accepted.

**A grant can pin a write action to dry-run.** A key whose `template:deploy` grant carries the dry-run floor cannot perform the write at all; the server previews it instead. Independently, any single write can be previewed per request by asking the control API for it, which returns what would have happened and changes nothing.

**Every auth-relevant action lands in the audit, attributable.** `GET /v1/audit` reads it, filtered, and reading it is itself a gated action.

**Internal service-to-service traffic can be mutually authenticated.** Set `service_auth: mtls` and rimsky stands up a per-deployment CA. Services enrol with their api-key over `POST /v1/enroll`, fetch the CA over `GET /v1/ca-root`, and renew their leaf certificates without an operator touching anything. Revoking the service's one key ends its access. A deployment that has not been hardened keeps working unconfigured.

**You can require transport security on a service entry.** An executor or claim-producer entry marked for TLS refuses a service that cannot present credentials, and the store side refuses to start rather than run unauthenticated.

Driven through: `rimsky auth *`, the `/v1/auth/*` routes, `POST /v1/enroll`, `GET /v1/ca-root`, `GET /v1/audit`, the `auth_*` and `audit_list` MCP tools, `service_auth` and the service `tls` config keys.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **No configuration turns anonymous mode off.** It is derived from the data: zero active keys means open. Keys such as `anonymous_mode: false` or `auth: {required: true}` stop the container at startup as unknown fields, and the environment equivalents are ignored. To guarantee a deployment never serves an unauthenticated request, mint a key before you expose it.
- **Key plaintext is shown once and is never retrievable.** `POST /v1/auth/keys` returns it in that response only. `rimsky auth show`, `GET /v1/auth/keys/{nameOrID}`, and the listing return the key's metadata and grant with no plaintext field, and no query parameter reveals it. Recover a lost key by rotating it.
- **Roles are a client-side expansion, not a server-side entity.** The server stores grants. A key created with `--role operator` reads back as sixteen grant entries with the word "operator" nowhere in it, and no route lists roles. The `role:` column the CLI prints is a match against the grant, so a key minted over HTTP with the same grant lists under the same role name.
- **Scope works on seven actions and one dimension.** `instance:create`, `tag:delete`, `tag:set`, `template:deploy`, `template:deregister`, `template:register`, and `template:undeploy` accept a scope, and the only dimension is `template_tag`. You cannot pin a key to one instance: `instance:read`, `instance:kill`, `message:send`, and the rest refuse both `instance_id` and `instance_key`. The refusal comes at key creation with the action and the valid dimensions named, so you never ship a key you wrongly believe is scoped.
- **The action registry is a closed set of 46 grantable actions.** `instance:update`, `asset:create`, `message:delete`, and sixteen similar guesses are refused at mint time as unknown actions — the operations behind them do not exist. Tag update lives under `tag:set`, not `tag:update`. Three further actions (`health:probe`, `service-auth:ca-root`, `auth:whoami`) are real but never grantable, because those routes consult no permission.
- **Wildcards are three fixed shapes, not globs.** `template:*` and `*:read` work. `instance:re*`, `inst*:read`, `*:*`, and eight further glob shapes are refused with the rule named. One sharp edge: a wildcard's noun is not checked against the registry, so `banana:*` mints successfully and grants nothing, while the literal `banana:read` is refused.
- **A key that lapses at its expiry emits no event.** Creation, revocation, and rotation each emit an audit kind; expiry does not, and there is no expiry kind to filter for. The lapse surfaces reactively as an `auth.access_denied` row with `denial_reason: expired_token` when some client trips over the dead key. The key's own row stays listed with its `expires_at`, and `GET /v1/auth/status` counts it out of the active total.
- **`POST /v1/enroll` and `GET /v1/ca-root` exist only when the deployment has a CA.** On the zero-config default, and with `service_auth: none`, both answer 404 to every caller — the router has no such path. They appear with `service_auth: mtls`, at which point the control API itself serves HTTPS.
- **`params_redact` covers the instance read, not the record.** `GET /v1/instances/{id}` returns `[REDACTED]`. The value stays in full in `GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/audit`, and the observability instance and event reads, because the audit row records the create request that carried it. Any holder of `event:read`, `audit:read`, or `observability:read` can read the value. Keep secrets out of params; pass them through the executor's own environment instead.

## The template catalog

**Rimsky keeps a catalog of registered templates and movable names for them.** You register a workflow definition, mark it ready to run, create instances from it, retire it so no new instances start, and remove it once nothing uses it. Registering the same template twice is idempotent and returns the same template id.

**Tags are movable names for a template hash.** You create a name, list the names and see what each points at, roll a name forward to a new definition and back again, and remove a name you no longer want.

**A template declares the message types its instances accept.** A declared type is accepted and reaches the node that reads it. An undeclared or non-conforming message fails loudly at the send, and a node that reads a message type the template never declared is refused at registration.

**Registration refuses a substitution the template does not cover.** A node that reads an upstream it never subscribes to is refused with the fix named, and the same finding is available before you attempt registration, through `rimsky template lint` and `POST /v1/templates/validate`.

**Instance creation validates against the services the template references.** The gate checks every referenced service, not just the first, and refuses a param value that breaks a referenced service's constraint.

**Your own validation services get to vet templates before they register.** A validator's blocking finding refuses the registration; an informational finding comes back as an advisory on a successful registration and on a validate call. You can make advisories blocking, so questionable declarations cannot register at all.

Driven through: `rimsky template *`, `rimsky tag *`, `POST /v1/templates`, `POST /v1/templates/validate`, the deploy and undeploy routes, `/v1/tags`, the `template_*` and `tag_*` MCP tools, the `messages[]` template keys.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **`rimsky template lint` needs a reachable deployment.** The verb uploads the file to `POST /v1/templates/validate` and the control API does the work, so with no deployment it fails with a connection error. This is structural: the findings name the operator's `executors:` and `claim_producers:` blocks, so the same file can lint clean against one deployment and fail against another. Lint does catch everything registration rejects.
- **Creating a tag is not idempotent, while registering a template is.** `POST /v1/templates` answers 201 then 200 with the same id, and creating an instance under one `instance_key` does the same. `POST /v1/tags` answers 201 then 409, and `rimsky tag create` exits 0 then 1. The idempotent form is `PUT /v1/tags/{tag}`, which updates but does not create — it answers 404 on an absent tag. A re-runnable deployment script has to choose the verb deliberately.

## Instances at runtime

**Creating an instance starts nothing.** A new instance is idle by construction. You invoke work as a separate operator action, so an instance's existence never implies a running graph.

**An empty message wakes every structural root.** Send a message that names nothing and rimsky starts the default work.

**You drive an instance's whole runtime lifecycle.** Create it, watch its progress, pause it, resume it, force-terminate one that is wedged, and remove its record once it is done.

**Every instance carries a message bus.** You send a message with a mandatory dedup key, read the instance's message history, fetch one message by id, and replay a send — a replay returns the original message rather than creating a second one.

**One message opens one frame.** Rimsky never merges two messages into a single frame, so substitution inside a frame is well defined. Each template chooses what happens to messages that back up behind a busy instance: `message_queue_mode` either keeps every pending wake or keeps only the newest.

**Forcing a re-run of a node that already has a run in flight queues it.** Rimsky does not drop the request and does not interrupt the run.

**You can inspect and reset one node.** You read a node's whole state on a running instance, and you clear a stale failure marker off a settled node — and nothing else.

**You can read a node's latest resolved attribute bag.** Both the node read and the observability node read return it.

Driven through: `rimsky instance *`, `rimsky node get`, `rimsky admin reset`, `rimsky messages tail|show`, `rimsky watch`, the `/v1/instances*` routes, `POST /v1/instances/{id}/messages`, `GET /v1/nodes/{id}`, `POST /v1/nodes/{id}/reset`, the `instance_*`, `message_*`, and `node_*` MCP tools.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **`rimsky admin reset` takes a node id, not an instance id, and asks nothing.** It demands exactly one argument and refuses an instance id with a not-found error. The control API narrows it further, refusing with 409 unless the node has a failed terminal run. It prompts for no confirmation: on a terminal with `n` waiting on standard input, it goes straight to the request.
- **Routes spelled `{id}` do not accept an instance key.** Seven `{idOrKey}` routes take either — the instance read, its nodes, breakpoints, breakpoint hits, pause, resume, and breakpoint create, plus terminate and delete. Ten `{id}` routes reject the key with 400 `invalid instance id`: frames, messages, assets, and the debug override. Resolve the key to a UUID first through `GET /v1/instances/{key}`.

## Authoring the graph

**Nodes fire on what upstream nodes emit.** A subscription names a signal type-path — exact, or a trailing-`*` prefix for a family — and optionally a CEL predicate over the payload. One subscription form reaches every signal an upstream can fire, and subscribing to a signal that cannot fire is refused before anything runs.

**A fan-in receiver waits for every upstream still in flight.** It dispatches once, after the last upstream completion, carrying values from all of them. Two force-refreshed upstreams on one node rendezvous rather than livelocking. A subscription can also declare that its sender be refreshed before the receiver runs.

**One predicate can fire on success and on error alike**, by predicating on the verdict's attributes rather than on the terminal kind.

**Held work cascades on resolution, not on dispatch.** A downstream subscriber sees an upstream's success only once the held claim commits, and hears an abandoned signal when the held work rolls back — reachable by exact name or through the broader error-family pattern.

**Cycles are first class.** A node can re-run against its own output until it converges, and a cycle of nodes can walk back to its start. The bundled `loop_counter` node bounds an iteration at a declared number of rounds and marks the terminal round, with no executor to write.

**Two idempotent cascade modes drop redundant re-runs.** `idempotent-queue` compares a node's inputs against its queued predecessor; `idempotent-settled` also compares against the most recent settled run. `most-recent` and `sequenced` are the other two modes.

**A node's execution unit can be a named sub-graph.** `delegate: <graph-name>` dispatches the sub-graph as one child execution; the calling node settles when the sub-graph settles and carries its outcome. A sub-graph declares its own `entry` and `exit`.

**A node can send a message.** `sends_message` builds an envelope from the node's attributes and puts it on the bus, which opens the next frame.

**Three utility node kinds dispatch in-process with no service deployed:** `loop_counter`, `attribute_passthrough`, and `send_message`.

**Substitution reads from every standard source.** A fan-out partition request reads from an upstream node's attribute, an instance param, a typed message body, the claim's own payload, or a host-environment variable. A message body is read wherever a node's attribute can be read, through one channel and one lookup, with the message and node namespaces kept apart — a mistyped reference of either form is refused before the template is usable. A claim's producer-supplied payload is read through the same directive on a regular claim and per sub-claim inside a fan-out. Marking a directive lenient makes a missing source resolve to empty instead of failing.

**A claim scope is substituted by its canonical spelling.** The canonical directive resolves to the live claim's scope. The abbreviated spelling is refused at registration, not at runtime, so a template that uses it never reaches a dispatch.

**Fan-out partitions one claim into many.** A declared fan-out splits a claim into one work unit per partition, the partitions really do run at the same time, and the parent settles on their aggregate verdict under an author-chosen policy: `strict`, `threshold`, `best_effort`, or `first`. A fan-out over an upstream list works the same way, as does a fan-out over the contents of a folder the filesystem store picked. Sub-claims inherit the parent's declared intent, so a read-only fan-out stays read-only.

**Error classes route by policy.** `error_types` maps a class to one of four actions: `pass` lets the run continue, `give_up` ends it immediately, `retry` bounds the attempts, and `release_and_requeue` sends the work back for another attempt. A producer's own declared acquisition class routes the same way, with the specific key winning over the generic `acquire/*` fallback.

**An executor's opaque bytes survive a recovery re-dispatch.** Rimsky carries them and never reads or rewrites them. An executor can also read, at dispatch time, whether this dispatch has no predecessor, follows a recalculated one, or follows one the runtime recovered.

Driven through: the template keys — `nodes[].subscribes[]`, `nodes[].cascade_mode`, `nodes[].delegate`, `nodes[].sends_message`, `nodes[].fan_out.*`, `nodes[].error_types.*`, `nodes[].claim_producers[]`, `nodes[].holds`, `graphs[]`, `messages[]`, `message_queue_mode`, `params_schema`.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **`error_types` has no catch-all.** A bare `*` and a `<prefix>/*` key each register with a vocabulary warning and match nothing at runtime, because policy lookup is an exact match on the class name. Declaring one fallback leaves every unnamed class on default handling. The one wildcard that works is `acquire/*`, the synthetic acquisition family. Enumerate the classes you mean.
- **Error classes are not uniformly prefixed and not a versioned catalog.** Eight classes rimsky raises itself carry no emitter prefix — among them `template_validation_failed`, `unresolved_executor`, `executor_sync_timeout`, and `abandoned`. Which classes are recognised depends on what the deployment's configured services advertise, not on a global list: `agent/refused` registers clean on a claude-agent node and warns on an http-node one. The capabilities handshake carries no version or deprecation marker.
- **Only `by_executor` attribute defaults can be written once in the template.** Rimsky resolves attributes per-executor, per-node, and per-match, and `attribute_overrides` on instance creation accepts all three. In the template, `by_node` and `by_match` fail at YAML parse. Per-node defaults have to be repeated on every instance creation.
- **`nodes[].tags` select over HTTP and nowhere else.** `GET /v1/instances/{id}/nodes?tag=team-a` filters by them. The CLI's `--tag` and `--tag-prefix` flags name template tags, not node tags, and are undefined on every verb that lists nodes — so reaching for `--tag-prefix` filters templates and returns a plausible empty answer. `rimsky instance nodes -o json` does not print node tags either.
- **The park controls are per-executor stub-mode probes, not a platform attribute family.** `probe_park`, `probe_cancel`, and `park_resume_at` register on any node. Only `http-node` and `claude-agent` park on them, and only when the executor process runs with `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_STUB_MODE=1`. `verifier-http` completes normally and `verifier-shape-checks` errors. Parked is a real runtime-wide node state; these attributes are not the way to reach it from a verifier.
- **`stub_response` does not exercise a graph offline.** It depends on an operator-set flag on the executor process, so a template author cannot turn it on. Even then, `http-node` honours it, `claude-agent` honours it only alongside `stub_probe: true`, `verifier-http` ignores it and returns a canned marker, and `verifier-shape-checks` fails asking for real data.

## Claims, locks, and data

**A claim is what a node acquires before it works.** A claim producer resolves the scope, hands back a handle, and rimsky drives the handle through the node's dispatch. Terminal resolution fires the producer's `Commit` or `Abandon` exactly once, under all four write semantics — `sync`, `staged_async`, `blocking_async`, and `read_only`.

**One claim can be shared across a whole subgraph.** `holds:` binds several nodes to one claim: it commits once when every node succeeds, and one node failing abandons the whole thing.

**A claim can outlive its dispatch.** `lifetime: durable` keeps the claim after the dispatch that took it ends. While it stands nobody else gets the scope, a later dispatch co-holds the same handle rather than taking a new one, and only a deliberate operator act releases it.

**The producer's own overlap rule decides who gets a claim**, on the ordinary path and on the fan-out path alike. A producer's declared refusal reaches the template as the producer's own error class, and a failing producer's class and message come back in what the operation returns.

**What the producer says on `Commit` is honoured.** The version id it returns lands on the claim handle, and its metadata reaches a fan-out parent's writeback under the partition's key.

**Two claim producers ship in the box.** `claim-producer-filesystem` gives directory-per-scope claims that write in place with no database, and fans out over what is already in the store. `claim-producer-postgres` gives staged-async claims: a batch becomes visible whole or not at all, each claimant gets a different row under a pick policy, a verifier check can gate a staged batch before it lands, and the producer declares its own error classes for templates to subscribe to.

**Named locks are a producer-independent capacity counter.** Acquisitions land on the same metric as producer-claim acquisitions, and lock saturation reads as its own series rather than being reconstructed from events.

**Assets are durable claims with a documented lifecycle.** You list the data assets an instance produced, see what an asset currently is, walk its version history, read the audit of how it came to be, trace what consumed it, and retire it once nothing needs it.

**Lineage is queryable in both directions.** You walk a run backward to what fed it and forward to what it fed, pivot from a claim handle into lineage and follow a claim to its sub-claims, ask which runs drew from a given source, and list everything a named producer committed. You prune lineage records older than a cutoff.

**Run records can leave the deployment.** The bundled OpenLineage subscriber delivers both the run DAG and the data lineage to an external receiver with no subscriber code written, and resumes at its cursor after a restart rather than replaying.

**A producer can carry the typed-data mix-in.** It stages one candidate per fan-out partition, finalized or collected, and surfaces version history through its own listing surface.

Driven through: the `nodes[].claim_producers[]`, `nodes[].locks[]`, and `nodes[].holds` template keys; the `claim_producers.<name>.*` and `named_locks.<name>.limit` config keys; the `/v1/lineage/*`, `/v1/instances/{id}/assets*`, and `/v1/claim-handles/{id}/holders` routes; `rimsky asset *` and `rimsky lineage prune`; the `asset_*` and `lineage_*` MCP tools; the ClaimProducer and DataProcessing gRPC protocols.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **Asset operations do not match across the three surfaces.** Four operations — list, get, versions, delete — exist on the CLI, the control API, and MCP. `rimsky asset lineage` is CLI-only: it is a client-side composition with no matching route and no MCP tool. Materialization history is the reverse — it has a route and an MCP tool but no CLI subcommand.

## The bundled services

Eleven services ship as images. Each is an ordinary service: rimsky reaches it over the same gRPC protocols your own services implement.

**`claude-agent` runs agentic work as a node.** The dispatch is handed off and settled later rather than held open. A node declares its own MCP servers under `cli.mcp_servers` and its own environment exposure under `cli.expose_env`, and the operator bounds both with `RIMSKY_CLAUDE_AGENT_MCP_ALLOWLIST` and `RIMSKY_CLAUDE_AGENT_EXPOSE_ENV_ALLOWLIST` — a node naming anything outside the bound fails that dispatch with the entry, instance, and node named. Exposed secret values do not land in the deployment's persisted state. A sign-off gate binds a signature to the output it covers. The agent's declared error classes route by policy or drive a subscriber. An agent conversation carries across re-fires inside one frame and starts fresh inside a delegated sub-graph.

**`http-node` integrates HTTP upstreams.** It issues a request and reads the response into the node's attributes, takes `error_class_field` to say which field of an upstream error body carries the error class, and can park the node on an upstream's rate-limit response.

**Two verifiers gate data.** `verifier-shape-checks` runs checks declared in node config against a claim's data, fails the node naming the check that broke, and fails loudly on a check kind it does not implement. `verifier-http` sends the check to an external service: an approving service lets the node settle fresh, a refusing one fails the node carrying the service's own class. Either way a finding labelled `warning` is recorded without blocking, and the same finding relabelled `error` blocks the commit.

**Four sensors turn the outside world into messages.** `sensor-cron` fires a declared schedule into the workflow with no scheduler of your own, and keeps its place across a restart. `sensor-http` polls a location and sends a message when the content changes, narrows a watch with a body filter, stays quiet on an unchanged body even after a restart, and refuses a private-range poll target until the operator allowlists it. `sensor-object-store` turns a deposit into work, hands each object to the graph exactly once, and treats only content inside the designated location as work. `sensor-webhook` turns an inbound call into a message with no poll in between, deduplicates a retried delivery, gates the endpoint with a shared credential, and accepts a signed call while refusing a wrongly signed or stale one.

**A publisher subscription is observable as it mounts.** You watch it go from mounting to active, and a create that succeeded against a missing publisher shows as a failed subscription rather than disappearing.

Driven through: the service images and their config keys; `publishers[]` in the template with `kind: cron | http | object-store | webhook`; the executor attribute keys; the `RIMSKY_*` service variables.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **The two allowlist families point in opposite directions.** Unset, the two `_EGRESS_ALLOWLIST` variables block loopback, private, link-local, cloud-metadata, and multicast destinations — closed by default. Unset, the two claude-agent allowlists permit everything, because zero-config local development runs that way. An unset allowlist is a closed door for egress and an open one for the daemon.
- **The egress guard covers two services.** `http-node` and `sensor-http` dial through it. `verifier-http` takes a URL from node attributes exactly as `http-node` does and has no allowlist variable at all, and the OpenLineage subscriber posts to whatever address it is configured with. A template author reaching an internal address through `verifier-http` is not bounded by either allowlist.
- **`RIMSKY_CLAUDE_AGENT_DISPATCH_MAX_USD` is a default, not a ceiling.** A node declaring `cli.max_budget_usd` gets its own figure, above or below the deployment variable. The variable applies only to nodes that declare nothing. An over-budget node is honoured, not refused.
- **The `auth` block works on the webhook publisher and is ignored on the HTTP one.** Registration, deploy, and mount all accept `auth:` on an `http` publisher, and then the sensor polls the upstream with no credential and no warning anywhere. The webhook publisher enforces it, and in fact refuses to mount without it.
- **`object-store: backend` names a local backend.** The build services `filesystem` and `memory`. Declaring `s3`, `gcs`, or `azure` leaves the subscription in `mounting` forever, with the sensor's refusal visible only in the orchestrator's log. `bucket` is a subdirectory of the operator's own root.

## Extending rimsky

**You write an executor.** It implements one unary `Execute` RPC. Rimsky discovers it from one declared endpoint, holds templates to the attribute schema it advertises, routes the errors it raises by the class it declared, steers subscriptions by the tags it declares, and settles on each terminal outcome it returns.

**You write a claim producer.** It implements open, commit, abandon, and release plus a capabilities handshake, and optionally `SplitScope` and `ScopesConflict`. Its startup advertisement reaches the deployment, it receives an open request already resolved against the instance, and its refusals reach the template as its own error classes.

**You write a publisher.** It feeds messages into a workflow, its subscriptions survive a deployment restart without being re-issued, and terminating an instance releases the subscription exactly once.

**You write a lifecycle subscriber.** Your service is told when templates are registered, deployed, undeployed, and deregistered, when instances are created and terminated, and when a run-scope reaches terminal.

**You write a validation mix-in.** Any service kind can advertise it, and the roles the service declares are the roles it is called for. An executor service vets the templates that use it; a publisher service gets the same vetting.

**You prove your implementation with the conformance kit.** `rimsky conformance` ships seven subcommands: `executor`, `claim-producer`, `publisher`, `validation`, `data-processing`, `lifecycle-subscriber`, and `probe`. A correct producer passes with nothing but the producer and the CLI; a failing one is told which checks failed rather than that it failed; a producer that claims staged-async but serializes internally is caught by a serialization probe. `--check-observability` covers the two observability protocols from their siblings' subcommands.

**Observability is optional and probed at startup.** An executor that implements it lets you fetch the whole trace for a finished dispatch and watch trace events arrive while a dispatch runs. A claim producer that implements it lets you page the producer's whole claim inventory, fetch one claim's full detail, stream claim-state changes as they happen, and render the custom admin views the producer declares.

**You can build a service without copyleft obligations.** The `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols` Go module and the `@rimsky-ai/protocols` npm package are Apache-2.0 and depend on nothing else in rimsky. A service built against protocols alone exchanges the protocol's verbs with a real deployment.

Driven through: the 10 proto files and their 36 RPCs; `rimsky conformance *`; the `executors.<name>.*`, `claim_producers.<name>.*`, `publishers.<name>.*`, `validators.<name>.*`, and `data_processors.<name>.*` config keys; the `/v1/observability/executors` and `/v1/observability/claim-producers` routes.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **Four of the nine protocols have no `Capabilities` RPC.** `ClaimProducer`, `ClaimProducerObservability`, `ExecutorObservability`, `Publisher`, and `DataProcessing` declare one. `Executor`, `Validation`, `LifecycleSubscriber`, and `HostDaemon` do not, and a client that opens every connection with a capabilities handshake gets `Unimplemented` against them.
- **Only two protocols have an observability sibling.** Executors and claim producers do. `publishers.<name>.observability_endpoint`, and the same key under validators and data processors, parse and start and do nothing — there is no such protocol and no such observability route. The configuration gives no signal.
- **HTTP+JSON is a bridge for two protocols, not a general transport.** `rimsky conformance claim-producer --transport http` works, and rimsky itself dispatches over an executor's HTTP bridge when the entry declares `transport: http`. Every other protocol is gRPC only, and the CLI says so. A claim-producer endpoint must be `grpc://`.
- **Two protocols have no conformance subcommand.** There is no `rimsky conformance host-daemon`, so a third-party host-daemon implementation has nothing to prove itself against. The two observability protocols are covered by `--check-observability` on their siblings rather than by subcommands of their own.
- **Conformance exit codes do not distinguish a failed check from an unreachable endpoint.** Both exit 1; only a usage error is distinct, at 2. No subcommand accepts `--json` or `--warnings-as-errors`, so CI has to parse the printed rows and the closing `N/M checks failed` line as text.
- **`@rimsky-ai/protocols` ships `.proto` files, not generated stubs.** The package exports `protoDir` and `protoPath` — a directory to point a proto loader at, and a function that joins a filename onto it. A TypeScript author still runs a protobuf toolchain over them.

## The local development loop

**One binary and one command run an ad-hoc template.** `rimsky run <file>` with no endpoint configured self-hosts the whole stack in-process, drives the run, and needs nothing else standing. `rimsky compose run <manifest>` does the same for a whole manifest: one invocation stands the run up and finishes it, with nothing to tear down afterwards.

**A one-shot run leaves a durable record.** Both the ad-hoc and the manifest-driven forms write a run artifact you can inspect after the fact.

**You see each node settle while the run is still going**, and the run's outcome is a branchable class: everything succeeded, something failed, or bounded out — distinguishable without parsing output.

**A binary named on the command line serves the run.** `rimsky run --service <name>=<path>` spawns the binary as a late-bound service for that run and it disappears with the run. Each binding takes its own environment, arguments, working directory, and spawn timeout. Sibling run-scopes in one frame get isolated child processes, and each child is reaped when its run-scope closes. A spawned binary must read `RIMSKY_DAEMON_PORT` and bind its gRPC server there.

**The host daemon runs the late-bind loop against a shared deployment.** `rimsky daemon start | status | stop` manages the daemon from the same CLI that drives the stack, tells you whether it is connected and what it is running, and stops it cleanly with its children reaped. The loop works before any credential exists, under anonymous mode.

**Concurrent developers stay isolated.** Each developer's instance dispatches only to that developer's own daemon, a second daemon joining does not knock the first one off, and a dispatch aimed at a daemon nobody is running fails rather than landing on somebody else's.

**A compose manifest drives many resources at once.** `compose plan` shows what the manifest would do, `compose up` applies it and applying it again repeats no work, `compose status` compares the manifest against what the deployment holds, and `compose down` removes everything the manifest created in one command. Manifest-created resources stay distinguishable from hand-authored ones.

**A newcomer copies the shipped example and drives it to completion.**

Driven through: `rimsky run`, `rimsky compose up|down|plan|status|run`, `rimsky daemon start|status|stop`, `rimsky ctx *`, the compose manifest keys, `late_bind_services` in the template, and `late_bind_service_proxies.<name>` in deployment config.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **`instances[].restart` is a reconciliation rule, not a supervision policy.** Nothing re-creates a terminated instance on its own; between applies there is no compose runtime at all, because `compose up` is a one-shot reconciler that exits. The key is read by the next hand-run `compose up`, where `restart: always` plans a delete-and-create and `restart: never` plans no change. `compose status` reports a terminated instance as in-manifest either way.
- **`templates[].state` only moves forward.** The legal values are `registered` and `deployed`; `undeployed` is refused outright, so the manifest stops working rather than undeploying anything. Setting a deployed template back to `registered` parses and does nothing. Removing an entry does remove the resource — but removing an instance entry while the instance is still live refuses the whole apply, blocking every other change in the manifest until the instance reaches terminal.
- **The compose family cannot authenticate.** `--endpoint` and `--key` parse on `compose status` and the credential is dropped, so the request goes out unauthenticated and comes back 401. `RIMSKY_API_KEY` fails the same way. The compose verbs work against a deployment in anonymous mode; against an authenticated one they do not, and the flag being accepted is what makes it silent.

## Watching, debugging, and auditing

**One chronological feed carries an instance's whole history.** You narrow it to one kind of activity or to a window of time.

**Every frame says why it opened** — an operator posted a message, a publisher delivered one, or the instance itself sent one.

**Every dispatch that finished says so in the ledger**, so durations come out of the ledger alone with no external timing.

**Four diagnostics read a wedged instance.** You read which nodes are parked, which frames the holding sub-graph is gripping, what the pending wakes are waiting for, and who currently holds a claim.

**Breakpoints stop a live instance.** You install one on a checkpoint of a running instance, see the hits it has taken, resume a stopped dispatch with an attribute changed, and delete the breakpoint and clear its hits.

**A debug channel overrides node state and attribute values.** You override on a paused instance, and you override at a breakpoint hit on an instance that was never paused.

**Executor traces are readable after the fact and live**, for executors that implement the observability protocol.

Driven through: `GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/audit`, the `/v1/admin/diagnostics/*` routes, the `/v1/instances/{id}/breakpoints*` routes, `POST /v1/instances/{id}/debug/override`, `/v1/observability/*`, `rimsky logs`, `rimsky watch`, `rimsky instance events`, `rimsky parked list`, and the `event_list`, `audit_list`, `breakpoint_*`, `held_frames_list`, `waitset_list`, `parked_node_list`, and `claim_holders_list` MCP tools.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **The diagnostics tell you why an instance is stuck and give you no lever to unstick it.** All four reads report the wedge accurately. There is no un-park route, no held-frame release, no producer-outbox retry, and no wait-set clear; `POST /v1/nodes/{id}/reset` refuses unless the node has a failed terminal run, and a debug override applies without unparking the node. The one action that clears the findings is terminating the instance.
- **`GET /v1/events` has no streaming mode.** With `Accept: text/event-stream` it answers a complete finite JSON response, and `?follow=`, `?stream=`, `?watch=`, and `?tail=` are accepted and ignored. `rimsky logs --follow` polls: one run at a 200ms interval issued five separate requests. Write a poll loop, and expect a full re-query per interval per watcher.
- **`kind` is an exact match, and the vocabulary carries three separator conventions.** Prefix filtering does not exist: `claim`, `subclaim`, `auth.`, and `claim*` are each refused with 400, while `claim/` parses as a signal type-path, answers 200, and matches nothing. The 44 kinds mix snake_case (`claim_acquired`), dots (`subclaim.acquired`), and slash paths, and one family is spelled both ways — `fan_out_dispatched` and `fanout.children_created` are both real.
- **Acquisition kinds do not pair with release kinds.** `lock_acquired` and `lock_released` pair. Nothing else does: a claim ends as `claim_resolution.commit`, `subclaim` has no release kind, and `claim_acquired` and `claim_held` are valid filter values that returned no rows across a run in which a claim was acquired, held, and committed.
- **Narrowing by node or instance silently drops the auth family.** `work_started`, `work_completed`, `attributes_substituted`, and the terminal kinds carry both identifiers. `instance_terminated` carries no node id, and `auth.access_attempted` carries neither — so filtering by node returns 200 with zero rows rather than saying the kind was excluded.
- **`/v1/observability/*` is a second read surface, not a read-only mirror.** It returns different shapes (`{"instance": …, "cascade_graph": […]}` against a top-level instance object), addresses nodes differently (`/v1/observability/nodes/{instance_id}/{node_type}`, with no by-node-id read), and carries fields the primary routes do not — including `terminated_at`, the field the delete route names in its own 409. It is also a different permission: a key granted only `instance:read` reads `/v1/instances` and is refused 403 on the observability twin. Events are the one genuine pair.

## Driving rimsky: choosing a surface

**The CLI talks to several deployments by name.** `rimsky ctx add|use|list|rm|current` registers deployments, shows which one is current, switches which one commands go to, and removes a registration without disturbing the others.

**MCP is a full second skin on the control API.** Its 57 tools reach 43 of the 44 permission actions the 61 HTTP routes reach, and reach nothing HTTP cannot. `observability_get` covers the whole observability family through one `path_suffix` argument. The catalog is computed per key: an admin sees 57 tools and a `*:read` key sees 30, with no mutating tool listed for the reader.

**The CLI carries no business logic.** Everything that dials is a pass-through, `template lint` included.

### Where rimsky differs from what you would expect

- **The CLI reaches about half the control API.** Some verb reaches 36 control-API routes; 32 are reached by nothing. Whole surfaces have no CLI verb: the debugger, pause and resume, the six lineage read routes, every observability route, the MCP transport routes, three of the four diagnostics, `GET /v1/audit`, `GET /v1/auth/whoami`, `GET /v1/runs/{run_id}`, enrolment, and message send — the CLI can tail and show messages but cannot send one. Choose HTTP or MCP when you need the whole platform.
- **`--json` is one verb; `-o json` is the other 25.** Of 30 read verbs, `rimsky auth list` takes `--json` only, 25 take `-o json` only, and 4 take neither. On any given verb exactly one spelling parses; the other exits 2 with an empty stdout, so `rimsky ls templates --json | jq` prints nothing and fails. A third meaning exists: `compose run --json` writes JSON Lines to **stderr**.
- **`-o` accepts two formats and silently accepts two more.** `human` and `json` are real. `-o yaml` is rejected by name; `-o table` and `-o text` are accepted and mean `human`, so asking for a table gets no error and no table.
- **Short flags do not generalise.** `-o` is a genuine short form of `--output`. `-f` is undefined on every verb carrying `--follow` or `--force`, and in the compose family it names the manifest path. Short forms do not cluster and take no attached value. `rimsky -v` prints the version, and `rimsky ls templates -v` is a parse error. `--yes` has no `-y`.
- **`--help` exits 2 on every leaf verb.** The root and the 14 family nodes exit 0; all 74 leaves print usage to stderr and exit non-zero, so a `set -e` wrapper around a help call fails. Six dev-loop shortcuts print the grouped verb's usage instead of their own, and `rimsky version --help` prints the version.
- **No verb asks before destroying anything.** Eleven destructive verbs — including `tag rm`, `instance delete`, `undeploy`, `template rm`, `auth revoke`, `asset delete`, and `lineage prune` — go straight to the request with `n` sitting unread on standard input. `--yes` is accepted everywhere and answers no prompt; on `instance kill` it stands in for `--force` and so enables a destruction. The one family that prompts is compose: `compose down` lists what it will do and asks. The one verb that stops is `instance kill` without `--force`, and it stops by refusing.
- **No CLI verb takes `--dry-run`.** The capability is real on the control API, which returns the preview envelope. The CLI has no spelling for it — `--dry-run`, `--preview`, and `-n` are undefined on all 31 write verbs — and worse, a key pinned to dry-run drives `rimsky deploy` to print "deployed" and exit 0 while the write never happened. Use the route, not the verb, when you want a preview.
- **Duration syntax is not one grammar.** Eight locally parsed flags take Go's grammar, so `30s`, `5m`, `1h30m`, and `500ms` parse and `30d` and `1w` do not. `auth create-key --expires` accepts `30d` and advertises it. `auth rotate --grace` rejects `30d` server-side. Config keys follow Go's grammar and fail hard — `dispatch_defaults.sync_rpc_deadline: 30d` produces a container that will not start.
- **Time-window flags are not uniform.** `--since` reaches 3 of 8 time-ordered reads, `--until` 3, `--older-than` 2, `--before` 1. `messages tail` takes no window at all, and `--until` on `watch` names an exit condition rather than a time bound. Where the flags do exist the grammar is strict RFC3339.
- **`--control-api` and `--api-key` are not the general spellings.** `--endpoint` and `--key` are, and even they are not universal — `ctx current`, `daemon status`, `daemon start`, and `compose run` take neither.
- **The error envelope has four shapes.** The core CRUD families answer `{"error": "<string>"}` with nothing machine-readable. The observability family nests it as `{"error": {"code", "message"}}`. `POST /v1/mcp` answers a JSON-RPC envelope. An unmatched path answers `404 page not found` as plain text and a wrong method answers 405 with an empty body. One route can use two shapes: the observability instance read is flat on 401 and nested on 404.
- **Status codes mostly hold and break in two places.** 401, 403, 404, and 409 map conventionally across eleven route families. An unknown instance id on the messages and claim-holders reads answers 200 with an empty list, so you cannot tell "no messages" from "no such instance". A malformed `?cursor=` — client input — answers **500** on five collection routes, so retry-on-5xx logic loops forever.
- **`DELETE` is not idempotent.** Every resource delete answers 404 on the second call, so a re-run teardown script exits non-zero on everything the first run removed. Success codes differ too (200 for tags, instances, and templates; 204 for breakpoints), and a live resource refuses with 409, which forces the order: terminate, delete instances, undeploy, delete template.
- **Pagination holds for eight collections and departs at the edges.** `/v1/instances`, `/v1/templates`, `/v1/events`, `/v1/audit`, `/v1/tags`, and the three observability collections all take `limit` and `cursor` and return `next_cursor`. The observability executors and claim-producers reads carry no cursor and ignore `limit`; `/frames` and `/messages` omit `next_cursor` on the last page; assets, breakpoints, and claim holders have no cursor field; breakpoint hits page on `since` and `next_since`. An empty page is `[]` on the core routes and `null` on the observability ones.
- **`/v1` is a path literal, not a negotiable version.** There is no discovery route, no version response header, and `/v2/health` answers the same 404 as a typo. The CLI concatenates rather than negotiating, so `--endpoint <base>/v2` requests `<base>/v2/v1/instances`.
- **MCP implements five methods and nothing else.** `ping`, `prompts/list`, `resources/subscribe`, `completion/complete`, `logging/setLevel`, and five more base methods answer `-32601 method not found`. `initialize` correctly advertises only `tools` and `resources`, so a client that reads capabilities is warned about everything except `ping`. Notifications are accepted and ignored, so a conforming client's handshake succeeds.
- **The `rimsky://` scheme is two breakpoint-hit forms.** Instances, nodes, events, templates, tags, and the audit log have no resource URI, and `resources/templates/list` is not implemented. The second documented form, `rimsky://breakpoints/{id}/hits`, resolves but is never listed. An agent that reaches for resources should reach for tools instead.
- **Two operations need HTTP even with MCP available.** `GET /v1/health` and `GET /v1/auth/whoami` have no tool, because both are ungated and the catalog is computed from the action registry. Both are what an agent asks first.
- **A listed MCP tool can still be denied.** For plain action-level grants the catalog matches the key exactly. Scope is evaluated per request target, so a key scoped to one template tag is shown `tag_delete` and gets 403 when it calls it on another tag. The same is true over HTTP; the boundary is the grant's shape, not the skin's.
- **Two teardown tools are named the inverse of their routes.** `instance_terminate` deletes an already-terminal instance and refuses a running one with 409; `instance_kill` forces a running instance terminal. On the wire, `POST /v1/instances/{id}/terminate` is gated by `instance:kill` and `DELETE /v1/instances/{id}` by `instance:terminate`.

## The codebase itself

**The project lints clean under its full comment and citation enforcement**, with both checks live rather than inert. **Every location the contributor rules cite is a real one**, and known-dead references stay out. These matter if you fork rimsky or send it a change; they say nothing about the platform's runtime behaviour.
